75,	to amend the Income War Tax Act (communicating information).

maintopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO COMMUNICATING INFORMATION
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
explain?
Mr. KNOWLES. This bill would add to the
appropriate section of the Income War Tax Act these words:
Provided that nothing in this subsection shall operate to prevent a minister of the crown from communicating to the Senate or to the House of Commons any information obtained under the provisions of this act.
It is quite conceivable that the restrictions as to secrecy imposed by subsection 1 of section 81 as it stands at present might have the effect of preventing a minister of the crown from giving the senate or the house such information as might be legitimately asked for and given. This amendment would also affect the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, since sections 40 to 87 of the Income War Tax Act are by section 14 of the Excess Profits Tax Act made to apply thereto.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: Before the house -rose for the Easter adjournment the Prime Minister undertook to give after the recess some indication as to the full programme of legislation from now until the end of the session. I wonder if the Prime Minister would take this opportunity of doing so.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: I shall not make mention of any of the measures already indicated on the order paper or referred to in the speech from the throne, nor of any of the measures which may arise out of reports of committees.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has referred to anything mentioned in the speech from the throne. Of course the speech from the throne covered so many matters with

respect to social security, health insurance and so on, that it would not be a very good explanation if we were to leave it at that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: I am referring only to specific measures there indicated. There will be a -bill to give effect to the extradition treaty with the United States; that comes under External Affairs but will be sponsored by the Minister of Justice. From the Department of Finance there will be the Canadian National Railways Financing and Guarantee bill; amendments to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and possibly an amendment to the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, or a separate bill. From the Department of Justice there will be amendments to the criminal code and a possible amendment to the Exchequer Court Act. From the Department of Labour there will be a bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act; from the Department of Mines and Resources a bill to ratify an agreement with the province of British Columbia regarding the administration of minerals within Indian reserves; from the Department of National Revenue come amendments to the National Revenue Act and from the Department of Naval Services there may be a slight amendment to the Naval Service Act.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: So far as the government knows at the moment, this is all that is in contemplation from now until the end of the session?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: Yes. I should say, of course, that as long as parliament is in session there is the possibility of some measure being introduced of which there has been no previous notice, but I have given my hon. friend a list that covers the ground so far as I am able to ascertain it at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide:
1.	That sums not exceeding one thousand million dollars ($1,000,000,000) be granted to His Majesty for the purpose of making war supplies available to any of the united nations.
2.	That the governor in council may determine the terms and conditions upon which such war supplies are made available to any of the united nations and may require in certain cases payment or repayment in kind or property or reciprocal action or provision of supplies or other direct or indirect benefit as may be deemed appropriate.
3.	That there be established a Canadian war supplies allocation board to carry out the purpose of this resolution, and that such board be authorized to employ officers, clerks and other employees necessary for the proper conduct of the business of the board.
4.	That the governor in council may be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, such sum or sums of money not exceeding in the whole the sum of one thousand million dollars ($1,000,000,000) as may be required for the purpose of defraying the expenditures herein mentioned and for purchasing or otherwise acquiring or procuring war supplies in Canada, the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I do not desire to address the house at the moment, but I should like to ask the minister if this perhaps is not the proper time for him to elaborate upon the general explanation which he made with respect io this bill on February 8.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I now propose to do so at some considerable length.
fMr. Mackenzie Kinjj.]
The house is already familiar with the general nature of this proposal. I outlined the substance of it in a statement to the house on February 8, summarizing several financial measures that were to be placed before parliament this session. To-day, on moving the resolution, I wish to summarize briefly the policy which it is proposed we follow and the general nature of the measures to implement it. I think we might conveniently leave discussion of the details until we are considering the bill itself and hon. members will then have the text of the bill before them. The resolution with which we are now concerned asks parliament to approve the provision of a billion dollars for the purpose of providing Canadian war supplies to our allies, and paves the way for the bill to make this appropriation and to establish the machinery for putting it into effect.
The general policy which it is proposed to follow in this Mutual Aid plan may be summarized under the four following points:
(1)	We wish to provide the war supplies which we are able to produce, over and above the requirements of our own forces, to our allies on the basis of strategic need, and we do not want any shortage of Canadian dollars on their part to make it impossible for them to obtain such supplies. In the term "war supplies" we include farm products and raw materials, which are necessary either for the production of munitions or for the maintenance of the services or civilian population of our allies.
(2)	We propose to enter into whatever reciprocal arrangements are practical, under which our allies will furnish us with supplies or services in return for what we provide, and we also take power to stipulate for the return to us after the war of any supplies or equipment furnished under Mutual Aid which appear likely to have a post-war usefulness. We do not propose, however, to provide aid only in those cases where it is possible to arrange for reciprocal aid, because in some cases this may be impracticable or undesirable. As I explained in February, it is an essential feature of this proposal that we may regard it as good and sufficient consideration for transferring war supplies to other united nations that such supplies are to be used in the joint and effective prosecution of the war.
(3)	We desire to avoid either piling up huge war debts by selling our supplies to our allies for payment after the war, or creating indefinite and uncertain post-war obligations which might arise out of transfers conditional upon undefined post-war considerations. It is for this reason that we have set out clearly in the

Mutual Aid Bill
bil! the essential feature which I have just mentioned, that is, that the effective use of the war supplies in the prosecution of the war may be deemed good and sufficient consideration for their transfer. Moreover, we intend where any terms and conditions are provided for to have these clearly specified at the time of transfer.
(4)	We propose to deal directly with the various countries requiring Mutual Aid from Canada and not to provide such aid to one country through the agency of another.
The working out of this Mutual Aid plan will not require the creation of much new governmental machinery. The bill will provide for the establishment of a board to make the necessary decisions or to recommend decisions to the governor in council. This board will consist of five cabinet ministers-the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Finance. It w'ill act as a committee of the cabinet under the chairmanship of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. It is expected that it will have a small administrative staff, but that most of the work resulting from its decisions and operations will be carried out by existing agencies. In procuring the war supplies to be transferred to allied nations, it will depend on existing procurement agencies, including not only the Department of Munitions and Supply but the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Fisheries and other agencies which have placed contracts or assisted in placing them with Canadian producers. The board will receive requests from various countries for Mutual Aid and consider the terms and conditions under which aid can be given to each country. May I say that when I use the term "Mutual Aid" I use it with capital letters, because the term has acquired in conversation somewhat of a technical sense. It really means aid, but we call it Mutual Aid; that is, the aid provided for under this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: If I may interrupt, the minister speaks of Mutual Aid having acquired somewhat of a technical sense. How did the technical term Mutual Aid arise, and why is it being used with capital initials?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: The bill is called the Mutual Aid bill, that is all. I announced that a month or two ago, and aid under the Mutual Aid bill is referred to in conversation as Mutual Aid.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: In other words the legal title of the bill will be the Mutual Aid bill. Is that it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Yes, exactly. The term is appropriate enough, because the principle underlying the bill is that this is aid to ourselves as well as aid to our allies.
In making these transfers the board will obtain advice on strategic needs from the appropriate military authorities. In judging how far a country is able to pay for what it requires from Canada, the board will obtain information regarding its balance of payment with Canada. All the details of the board's procedure and functioning are naturally not yet worked out in full, but I do not anticipate very much delay in its coming into operation once parliament has approved the necessary legislation.
This Mutual Aid plan is the logical conclusion of the development of our previous financial policies. From the beginning of the war we have been providing our allies with war supplies of various kinds, including raw materials and foodstuffs, in large volume. From the first few months of the war we have had to take special measures of one kind or another to enable our allies to obtain these supplies from us. This Mutual Aid plan is the latest of such measures and follows logically from the others.
Up to the present we have dealt primarily with Britain in giving this aid to our allies. AVe have provided assistance to Britain not only to meet her own requirements but also to meet those of the rest of the sterling area, which is composed chiefly of the British dominions, India, the British colonial empire and certain other middle eastern areas. The dollar exchange resources of Britain and the rest of the sterling area are pooled. Parts of the sterling area which receive a surplus of dollar exchange from operations with Canada turn that surplus in to this pool and when they require dollars for expenditures in Canada they obtain them from this pool. The foreign exchange control systems of the various parts [DOT] of the sterling area are more or less unified for this purpose. Consequently in the past it has been convenient to provide dollar exchange to Britain which places it in the pool of dollar resources available for the use not only of Britain but of other parts of the sterling area. Moreover, we have provided goods to Russia through Britain inasmuch as Britain, made direct arrangements with Russia very soon after Russia came into the war to supply Russia with various munitions of wrar and raw materials, and we have provided Britain with some of these supplies which she in turn has passed on to Russia in accordance with the terms of her protocol.
We are now proposing to deal directly with these other countries rather than through
Mutual Aid Bill

Britain as a channel. These other countries will include not only various British dominions but also Russia, China and other united and associated nations which are in need of this type of assistance. We have now direct diplomatic and supply contacts with Russia and China as well as with the various British dominions concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Is it intended that this flow of supplies to Britain shall cease and not come under this arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: So that the whole of the balance is used up now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Yes; it was exhausted at the end of last December.
The balance of the deficit was met by temporary arrangements which I shall describe in a moment and which applied to the later months of the year. During the nine month period of the billion dollar contribution to Britain, that contribution and the other means of financing the sterling area payments to Canada enabled us to transfer to the ' sterling area munitions, war equipment and defence services to a total value of $740 million; foodstuffs $242 million; and raw materials and other commodities amounting to $288 million.
, In the several months that have elapsed since the billion dollar contribution has been completed, the sterling area deficit has been covered by means of two interim arrangements which were available only as temporary sources of funds until we could get this Mutual Aid plan into operation. The first of these interim methods used was payment by Britain of her Canadian dollar deficit for a short time by the transfer of United States dollar balances which Canada was able to utilize in the United States. The second method is one with which the house is familiar. We purchased from Britain her investments in Canadian war plants which had been made through the capital assistance programme of the Department of Munitions and Supply. It will be recalled that $200 million was voted for this purpose in the supplementary war appropriation for the last fiscal year. These funds have been paid over to the account of the British government and have met their requirements in the last month or two, and will probably carry them through a considerable part of this month.
The house will also recall that Canada has undertaken to meet the full cost of maintaining thirty-five additional R.C.A.F. squadrons overseas and to meet the full cost of the pay and allowances of R.C.A.F. personnel serving in R.A.F. squadrons overseas. This increase in our expenditures in Britain and the rest of the sterling area will reduce by about $40 million per year a sterling area
deficit of Canadian dollars. It is also expected that our military expenditures in Britain will be considerably higher this year than they were in the past. This increase in the sterling expenditures of our armed forces will probably be considerably greater than any increase in British payments to Canada this year over previous years, particularly as a larger proportion of our war production in Canada is now going to our own forces rather than to the British forces. Consequently the probable excess of the sterling area's payments to Canada over its receipts of Canadian dollars will be substantially less this year than they were last year.
While, therefore, the interim measures that we have taken have tided over the period since, last December and the increase in our expenditures abroad will reduce the deficit to be covered to more manageable proportions, nevertheless a quite considerable problem remains in providing supplies not only to Britain, Russia and China, but ' to other British dominions and to other parts of the sterling area as well. It is to meet this continuing and general problem that the Mutual Aid plan is proposed.
This system of Mutual Aid will enable our great productive power, industrial and agricultural, to be most fully and effectively used in the prosecution of the war. It will enable us to exert a balanced effort in accordance with the nature of our own resources-the type of effort that we are best able to make quickly and effectively.
Because of our natural resources, particularly in agriculture, and our great industrial capacity which has been so rapidly increasing in the last few years, and also because of our relative safety from direct enemy attack, we are able to produce far greater quantities of war supplies than our own forces require. These can and should be furnished to our allies. It would be inequitable and wasteful from the point of view of the united nations' war effort as a whole if our allies were unable to obtain what they require from us and we attempted to reduce oUr production to the point where we ourselves utilized all that our allies were not able to buy from us with the cash at their disposal.
The products of our factories and our farms, of our mines and forests and refineries, should go where they are most immediately effective in wining the war-where they will be most effective in saving our lives and the lives of our allies. The disposition of these supplies to the places where they are most useful should not be prevented by any inability on the part of our allies to pay Canadian dollars for what we should send to them. It is our enemies whom the. Chinese have fought so desperately and at such terrible cost year after year in Asia. Their sacrifices undoubtedly will have saved thousands of Canadian lives. But we do not share even the material cost of their forces let alone the terrible misery that they have endured. Surely in these circumstances we should not be niggardly in fixing the terms on which we supply to China what we can and, I must add, what can be transported to her.
This Mutual Aid plan which the government is proposing is similar to what is being done now by other countries which are in a position to furnish supplies to their allies. We are all familiar in a general way with the Lend-Lease Act and the aid which the United States is giving under this act to nearly all the united nations. This epoch-making measure was conceived by Mr. Roosevelt and enacted by the United States congress while the United States was still a neutral. Our Mutual Aid plan is somewhat similar in principle. I hope it will prove a little simpler in application. It is naturally different in some respects because our plan is introduced while we are at war, with the American experience as a guide, while theirs, as I have said, was introduced before they were a belligerent.

Mutual Aid Bill
I think it would interest the house to recall some of the salient features of the United States Lend-Lease Act, the reasons for it, and the results that have been achieved under it. I think I can do this best by quoting a short passage from the report to congress by the lend-lease administrator, dated January 25, 1943.
This report begins with these words:
The Lend-Lease Act was enacted by the congress as a measure of national defence on March 11, 1941, nine months before the threat of axis attack upon us materialized at Pearl Harbor. Full and lengthy public hearings and debates on the issues preceded passage of the law. Recognizing the threat against us, the United States in substance affirmed that:
(a)	It was essential to our security that all possible material assistance be furnished to those nations then fighting or threatened by the axis.
(b)	It was in our interest that the flow of weapons and other supplies furnished to permit the defence of the United States should not be interrupted by a lack of dollar exchange.
(c)	Since aid was being furnished in our own defence and it was important to avoid the international debt experience of the last war, payment might be made in kind or property or other benefits, rather than in dollars.
A little further on:
Under the act, the President is authorized by congress, "in the interest of national defence," to procure and provide "defence articles" and "defence information" for the government of any country whose defence he deems "vital to the defence of the United States." Defence articles and defence information are defined to include all types of goods and services necessary for the waging of total war. The act provides that "the terms and conditions under which any such foreign government receives any aid . . . shall be those which the President deems satisfactory, and the benefit to the United States may be payment or repayment in kind or property, or any other direct or indirect benefit which the President deems satisfactory."
Lend-lease is not a loan of money. Nor has it ever been an act of charity. The lend-lease programme of providing goods and services to nations resisting the axis aggresors was undertaken for the defence of this country and has been carried out in the interests of the people of the United States. We have aided peoples under lend-lease because their interests coincided with our interests.
When the lend-lease act was passed, there was still the possibility that by putting the full weight of our economic resources behind those countries fighting the axis, the defeat of the aggressors might be secured before we ourselves were attacked. Pearl Harbor ended that possibility. The axis attack upon us vindicated the wisdom of lend-lease policy.
By beginning the lend-lease programme when we did, we greatly strengthened ourselves. We strengthened the nations w'hose fight was keeping axis aggression from this . hemisphere. We strengthened _ our inner defences as well.
Great Britain, then standing rjone, was assured of a continuous and mounting flow of arms and food from the United States. China,
[Mr. Ilsley.l
then in its fourth year of heroic resistance to Japan, was assured more American supplies over the Burma road. After the Soviet Union was attacked, lend-lease support was assured the Red armies then battling desperately before Moscow.
Then a little later:
The basic war strategy of the united nations is to combine all their material and man-power resources in such a wrny as will achieve the maximum possible impact upon the enemy in the shortest possible time. Lend-lease is a principal means by which the United States combines a share of its material strength with the material strength and man-power of our allies in order to carry out this strategy.
When a General Sherman tank smashes through an axis emplacement, the enemy is hurt just as much, whether the action is before Stalingrad or on the axis flanks in Libya and Tunisia. An American-made fighter plane strikes effectively in the cause of the united nations whether it is strafing the Japanese in occupied China or the nazis in occupied France.
American steel shaped by British machine tools into 25-pounder guns at a factory in the English Midlands adds to the total fire power of the armies fighting the axis. The same is true of American tools machining Indian steel into shells in a factory in the central provinces of India.
American foods shipped abroad bring the day of victory closer by providing the calories necessary to sustain the energy and strength of those fighting our enemies, whether it be a soviet soldier from Tiflis pushing forward against the nazis through snow and ice-or a dockyard worker who went through the London blitz and is now unloading supplies for United States forces in Britain-or a British mother whose children are entrusted to a day nursery while she takes a man's place at a lathe in a shellmaking plant.
Lend-lease supplies in the hands of the other united nations serve the war effort of the United States.
And a little later:
Lend-lease transfers have been authorized of goods and services procured from regular army, navy and maritime commisison appropriations up to a maximum value of $35,970,000,000.
That is the total authorization up to the date of this report by Mr. Stettinius. Then a little later:
The total value of lend-lease aid in 1942 amounted to $7,009,000,000, consisting of goods transferred in an amount of $5,637,000,000, and services rendered in an amount of $1,372,000,000. This was more than five times the total for 1941. In the last three months of 1942 alone, the value of lend-lease aid was $2,482,000,000, twice the total for all of 1941.
Tfic cumulative value of lend-lease aid from March 11, 1941, to December 31, 1942, was $8,253,000,000. Of this amount 79 per cent Was for goods transferred and 21 per cent for services rendered.
Then later on:
Measured in terms of money spent, lend-lease represents about one-eighth of the total United States war effort. This country spent for all war purposes $63,408,000,000 from March 1, 1941, to December 31, 1942. The value of lend-

Mutual Aid Bill
lease aid during the same period was $8,253,000,000 or 13 per cent. 1942 munition exports, including both those made under lend-lease and those by direct purchase, were 19 per cent of total United States munitions production. For the last six months these exports have been running at about 15 per cent of production.
We have sent considerably more than 19 per cent of certain combat weapons to the other united nations. Of our 1942 production of tanks and combat planes, excluding cargo planes, trainers, etc., we have shipped, both under lend-lease and by direct cash purchase, about one out of every three to our allies. These weapons were most urgently needed on the battle fronts of 1942. On the other hand we have sent less than 15 per cent, or none at all, of many other items.
And later:
Agricultural products, most of them foods, exported under the lend-lease programme from March 11, 1941, to November 30, 1942, were valued at $1,329,000,000.
I think that is sufficient to quote from that report, but I wanted to read that to the house to show the extent of the aid the United States is giving on principles similar to those laid down in this bill, and the reasons they have given publicly for putting their aid in that form.

My purpose in rising at this time is to see if we cannot engender into the cold facts and figures a spirit which will be reflected in enthusiasm in the minds and hearts of our people on the farms, in the forests and in the factories, and which will affect all those who provide those extra supplies so badly needed.
May I say frankly that I am disappointed in the minister's statement. It does not go far enough. It does not give us enough detail. It does not tell us how many tanks and planes are being supplied, how much foodstuffs is being supplied, or anything of the kind. There is no break-down of figures. From last year's bill the minister had a model to follow, because at that time we gave SI,000 million to the United Kingdom. He said in his statement that already the machinery is set up from last year to proceed with allocating the present $1,000 million to the united nations. Well, if that machinery is set'up why are there not produced to this chamber the results attained by last year's expenditure, when that $1,000 million has been completely spent? Why have we not some detail, as we had when we dealt with the balance required for war expenditures? I believe war expenditures were set out in Voles and Proceedings of March 2.

I appreciate the minister's difficulty, and I must say I am in accord with a certain amount of censorship. But if we can find from United States records what has been done under their lend-lease appropriations, and if we use those figures to engender enthusiasm in the hearts of our people, by pointing out that one dollar out of every three dollars went toward the purchase of tanks for the united nations, then why can we not do something of the kind in describing Canada's appropriations? Why can we not point out, for instance, that one dollar out of every three has been spent in the production of tanks, the production of aeroplanes or the like, for the benefit of our allies of the united nations?
The point I am making is that we need facts of this kind to satisfy and engender
I Mr. Ilsley.]
enthusiasm in those of our people who are responsible for the production, those who are doing the work. It is not enough always to speak negatively. It is not enough for the minister to suggest that the production of bacon and cheese might be cut down. We must look at the positive side of the picture at every opportunity and encourage our people to produce more and more. We must not be content to look at the negative side. I am in accord with the four points raised by the minister. I believe the house will agree with him. But I am anxious to point out to our people that we are really doing something worth while, and intend to do more, provided of course that there is no shortage of Canadian dollars.
How satisfactory it would be if we could rise in our places and point to the experience we had in respect of the $1000 million credit which was exhausted in December last, and say to our people in the farming community, "You provided one-third of that S100O million credit. You made it possible that China might be fed. You made it possible that North Africa might be fed." How satisfactory it would be to be able to say that those goods went to Britain. We know that Britain had a protocol with Russia, and she was able to make financial arrangements by transferring our goods, in turn, to Russia. At the same time, not through our- generosity but simply in carrying out our duties to civilization, we let sterling balances accumulate in London and negotiated an interest-free loan. That was the very least we could do. How satisfactory it would have been if we could have had the facts with respect to that situation. That was a reciprocal arrangement. We are now on the debit side. Even $1000 million is not enough to pay for . the blood and energy that is being expended on the fronts holding the enemy back from our shores. In a business sense it is quite all right to have these reciprocal arrangements. But we have had experience, in that we gave $1000 million last year. We must give some explanation with regard to that arrangement, and the apportionment of the money, if we are to satisfy those of our people who take such a narrow view in respect of present world conditions. We must have something tangible to show for any reciprocal arrangement or for materials given. That being so, let us have the facts, and we can answer them. Thank God there are only a few such people in Canada, only a few who are worrying as to whether we are getting dollar for dollar. If in our discussions we could give facts respecting these transactions I believe they would prove helpful.

Mutual Aid Bill
It would be desirable to have information with respect to the return of goods in the post-war period. And not only that; I should like to see a return to this country even now of those businesses and manufacturing establishments in Great Britain which have been wrecked, but which in all probability will not be rehabilitated over there. Why not begin bringing them to Canada, right now? For example, why not bring a score of technicians who are over sixty-five years of age? If they are not essential to industry in Great Britain, have them brought to Canada. Let us bring to Canada too the people who have increased their agricultural production, but who, perhaps because of a shortage of supplies and lands, have found that they are not operating economically. Let them produce foodstuffs in Canada. In this country they could produce twice as much at the same cost and by the expenditure of the same energy. If the problem were presented in this way I believe our people in Canada could be stirred to even greater effort.
We know from experience of other days that a lot of post-war debts are not collectable. I think it would be far better to have any post-war debt in the hands of the United Kingdom than in the hands of others with which we have not had as much experience. In her dealings with Russia, in her dealings with China, in her plan of dealing generally, protocol or whatever you may like to call it, in her commercial actions, in her trading, in her shipping and what-not, the United Kingdom is in a much better position than we are. I cannot see why this change has been made, why we switched from the United Kingdom to the united nations.
If it is going to be of some benefit in connection with the activities and goodwill and the live and let live policy, or the other philosophy which the minister so often mixes in with his speeches, then it is all right; I am satisfied. But I am still of the opinion that the United Kingdom is in a better position to distribute our surplus production of one kind and another than we will be under this united nations plan. So far as the collecting of sterling balances in sterling areas is concerned, the United Kingdom knows where they are. She is dealing with these matters in greater magnitude than we are, and I suggest that we should let her do it.
If we consider we have risen to nationhood and are going to do this ourselves, many of us are of the opinion that the sterling balances which we may accumulate from New Zealand or from Australia, where the currency is on a little different exchange base from that established in our United Kingdom agreement
last year, will mean another set of bookkeeping, another set of settlements. So far as commonwealth sterling balances are concerned, if necessary we should be ready to make interest-free loans to those countries which are not able to export back to us sufficient goods to create their own Canadian balances. I am of the opinion that many of these countries will not be able to do this.
I gathered from the minister that this $1,000 million to the united nations probably will not be enough, because in all probability the United Kingdom itself will require more than it had last year. Last year the United Kingdom exhausted its $1,000 million by December. If that is so, we must not under any circumstances stop or halt in our stride; we must not slow down in any way. Do not let it be thought, among our agricultural communities particularly, that we might not be able to export whatever agricultural surpluses we have because the division of this SI.000 million among the United Kingdom and the other component parts of the united nations may not permit them to buy all our surplus production.
I am in accord with direct dealing if it will stimulate and invigorate our people and bring about greater production. I do not like to mention the rumours that are abroad, but the government should spike one rumour. It is being said that Great Britain resold to some of the other component parts of the united nations, perhaps at a profit, some of the goods she obtained under the gift of $1,000 million which was made last year. A statement should be made by the administration dispelling that rumour. The gossips say that New Zealand and Australia felt that they had to pay a premium for some of the gift of Canada that found its way to them.
In my opinion we should have a breakdown of the $1,000 million. Not that we are niggardly-I do not like to use that word here; not that we want to deal harshly with the united nations. That is not our idea. Far be it from any one in this chamber to get into that frame of mind. Just the reverse is the case. We find in Votes and Proceedings the following statement made in connection with the total expenditure of $4,558,000,000:
Payments for the account of the government of the United Kingdom to enable it to purchase in Canada aircraft, tanks, mechanical transport vehicles, guns, ammunition and other munitions of war, foodstuffs, raw materials and other commodities and supplies essential to the conduct of the war and the maintenance of the people of the United Kingdom, and to defray other expenses incurred in Canada arising out of the war, $1,000,000,000.

We should have a detailed breakdown, not only of this estimate of $1,000 million, but of the United Kingdom billion as well. Then, as I said at the beginning, we shall be able to encourage our people to more and more production. We shall be able to tell them what they have done, not only for the United Kingdom but for China, for Russia and ' for the other component parts of the united nations. We can exhort them to do even more, particularly the farmers who at this time of year are thinking about what they are going to produce in the coming season.

Mr. Speaker, I was rather hoping that the debate would be adjourned this afternoon so that we might have an opportunity of looking over the complete statement the minister has made. However, I take it that we shall be able to go into the details of this appropriation when we are discussing this resolution in committee or on the bill itself; consequently if we confine ourselves to general remarks we shall be doing all that is necessary at this time. I noticed that the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) confined himself to a few major points.
On behalf of the party with which I am associated I should like to say that we support unhesitatingly the idea of a gift to the united nations. We believe that Canada is in a favoured position. So far throughout the war we have been remote from devastating air raids and we have suffered relatively little from the impact of war. True, we have lost a number of splendid boys in the air, on the sea and in the army, but none the less the civilian population of this country has been exceedingly fortunate in escaping the difficulties and hardships which others of the allied nations have had to encounter.
I notice that the minister, in reply to a suggestion of the hon. member for Danforth

that we should go into the details of the gift made last year and what it is proposed to do this year, said he would be prepared to do so, or words to that effect, provided that the censorship regulations would permit. If that is the case, if in this house we are to be subjected to a censorship of discussions of expenditures of funds that have been raised by parliament for the purposes of war; if we cannot discuss these expenditures publicly, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we have a real case for a secret session at which these expenditures can be brought before the house and the house judge as to the necessity for publicity or otherwise. My own opinion is that we are not in this parliament sufficiently well informed as to the policies that are being pursued, both in relation to our external affairs as a nation and in relation to some of the commitments and the expenditures that we are making. I suggest	that we	are	no
longer in that stage of our development; that Canada is a nation and must assume her obligations as a nation. What we do as a nation we should do as a nation. We cannot always expect, if I may put it in this way, to hang on to mother's apron strings. The time has come when we should adopt the more direct policy which the minister has suggested this afternoon.
I do not agree with the minister that we should not repatriate Canadian securities that [DOT] are now	held	in Great	Britain.	Let	usremember that the repatriation of these securities	will	make no	difference	to	thecommon	people	of Great	Britain. It might

But in the course of his remarks this afternoon the minister made a brief reference to Canadian securities held in Britain. Last year we gave one billion dollars to Great Britain, and were glad to do it. We are giving another billion dollars this year, and we are glad to do it. In addition we made a loan last year of S700.000.000 to Great Britain, without interest, for the duration of the war, and we were glad
to do it. But it seems to me that in our own public interest we should be seeing that against the loans, not against the gifts,' we should be devising ways and means of getting out of debt as a nation and as institutions.
I personally think that in making financial arrangements we should protect the country to that extent. That is our duty, I take it, as members of this House of Commons. I should be prepared to go beyond the billion dollars in the way of a gift. I do not mind, when we are assuming our share in this war, giving all that we ought to give, but in making loans I believe that we have a right to protect the interests of this country, both in regard to the loans and in regard to the securities that are now held across the seas.
I have noted what has been done in this connection by several of our sister dominions and the great dependency of India-India, which, let it be remembered, is still under British authority, the portfolio of finance being I understand in the hands of a British appointee and citizen. It would enable us to settle some of the transportation problems which may beset us after the war is over. I have no hesitation therefore in saying what I have said this afternoon, and in urging

that we try, when the opportunity is at hand, to free our people to that extent from exploitation.
There are several questions which I intended to ask the minister in connection with these securities and their taxation position. I put some questions on the order paper-I filed them last night-and when the time comes and we are in committee we can elucidate these points.
While I have expressed this point of view this afternoon, we of this group and this movement are in favour of granting all the aid that we can grant to Great Britain and to our allies. We should give more than we have given, but in giving, we divorce from our thinking the question of the control of institutions in this country by various financial and capitalist groups in Great Britain. I do not wish to say more this afternoon, because we shall have an opportunity of studying the statement. We should give all we can to the allied nations, and particularly Russia, which has borne the brunt of the war in the last two years; and not only to them, but to China. I do not know how we can get more supplies to China, but in my opinion every effort must be made to do so. I had the privilege not long ago of meeting a group of well-informed Chinese gentlemen from Chungking, and I know perfectly well that they are in dire need. It is no secret that their food supplies are entirely inadequate; it has appeared in the public press; therefore I repeat that the rise in price of rice, their staple article of food, amounted by last December I am told to something like 800 per cent in the past few years. It is indeed fortunate that we have vast supplies of grain, vast supplies of foodstuffs, if we could only get them to those who need them.
In closing I would emphasize again that these great supplies of grain, which seemed to so many like a millstone around our necks, are to-day one of our greatest assets, one of the greatest assets of our common cause. Those of us who have been out west during this Easter vacation and who have seen vast heaps of grain lying in the open, who

I should like to suggest this to the membership of the house as the basis upon which this measure might and should be justified. The ultimate objective of this measure is the destruction of the common enemy, and for that reason I intend to support the resolution before the Chair. I deprecate the idea that this is a gift. I suggest that it is a contribution to the common cause, and as such it is entitled to our wholehearted support. I regret that there are certain schools of thought, not many I hope in this fair Dominion of Canada,
who are not receiving the idea in that sense. I am not going to be specific about this, but I have read certain controversies in certain parts of Canada suggesting that this country should not contribute, in the common cause, to a nation that was perhaps wealthier than ours.

Or nations that were wealthier than ours. I do not think that is the basis upon which the billion dollar vote was made last year, nor do I apprehend from the minister's statement to-day that it is the basis upon which this contribution is being made. We are making it for our own protection and defence, and I should like to remind hon. members of the stand I took last year in connection with the grant, or gift, or whatever you wish to call it-the previous legislation which authorized the raising of one billion dollars in the common effort. Speaking on that bill on March 18, 1942, I expressed the hope and wish that the measure would receive the unanimous support of the house and the country. I said that the proposal before us was much more than a gesture; it was a tangible recognition of an obligation the payment of which was long past due by Canada. And as the tragic struggle has proceeded in the intervening period of time, as the tempo of the war has increased, it is but natural that the government of this country, giving to the country the leadership so absolutely necessary in a time of stress and strain, should promote measures which would have the effect of aiding the common cause in the best possible manner through the best means that we can provide to that end. I suggest that the true principle under which this measure should be justified is to regard it as a contribution to the common cause for which we are all fighting. On that basis I intend to support the measure.
When the proper time comes I shall deal with some of the statements contained in the resolution itself and with the statements made to-day by the minister. The minister made a rather long and important statement. I think it is due to the membership of this house, who have not had an opportunity of studying that statement, that some little time should be given in order that we might analyse it and understand the import of some of the remarks he made and some of the basic considerations to which he referred. May I say to the minister that he made a strong argument in support of the bill, but I felt that it was a sort of apologia for the bill, that he anticipated an attack against the principle of

Mutual Aid Bill
it. I hope that was not in his mind; I hope he will feel that the united support of the people of Canada is behind the principle underlying this measure, namely that it is one more evidence that Canada will contribute to the utmost of her ability to the common cause. I hope he will not feel in any sense apologetic toward any unimportant branch of public opinion in Canada which may be critical of the principle he has .enunciated to-day.
I think we must all bear in mind that while Canada already has made great material contributions to the common cause, the fact still remains that the Canadian army has not yet been in action, that the fighting has been done by others as far as the armed forces are concerned. I use that expression in its limited sense, not to include the magnificent work of the Canadian navy and not meaning to include what I consider our most heroic contribution to the whole war to date, namely, the effort of our air force in which I include the heroism of hundreds of young Canadians who have given their lives in this strenuous warfare during the last few weeks. I am not unmindful of the episode at Dieppe and the heroism which our men displayed there. When we come to the consideration of the war appropriation measure I intend to ask some questions of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) with respect to Dieppe, arising out of a speech which he made in the city of Ottawa not very long ago before a veterans' association. I shall not pause here to refer to it, but I should like to say that I think the minister ought to have been a little more specific in his statement with regard to the principles which will actuate the ministry in the allocation of the material aid which is to be provided by this bill. I caught a few phrases as the minister went along. He said these goods were to be allotted on the basis of strategic needs; I think that was the term he used.

speechtext:
He said a committee of the cabinet was to be set up, which would be all-powerful in the distribution of these goods. On what theory, on what basis and for what reasons would a committee of the cabinet decide a question of strategic need? It would seem rational to assume that it would be on some basis which would not be determined here in Canada, because it would seem to me absolutely impossible that we could have the detailed information that would be necessary to decide what was equitable and just in the matter of distribution; that it must be upon the basis of information coming to us from the allied war command. In that
connection, how useful it would be if we had some sort of supreme council on which Canada could be adequately represented, which could give advice and suggestions to the cabinet committee which is proposed to be established as to the distribution of these supplies.
This is to be patterned, I gathered from the minister, more or less on the principle of lend-Iease; that is to say, there are to be reciprocal provisions the details of which have not been actually settled as yet. Well, I do not think there is any objection at all to incorporating reciprocal provisions into this bill or into the regulations which may be set up under it, but I think the House of Commons of Canada should1 know when the time comes, in committee on this resolution or in committee on the bill, just what the ministry has in mind in this connection with respect to reciprocity. What have these other people to offer us? I should not like to put the acceptance of this measure by this house or by the people of Canada on the basis that we are to get reciprocal aid. As far as I am concerned I would never vote for a measure based on the theory that because we give we ought to get something back. Let me come back to the main thesis I had in mind, that this is a contribution to a common cause, given freely by the Canadian people under leadership given by the ministry of this country charged for the time being with the responsibility of administering Canada's war effort, and that we do it because we are grateful for what others have done for us. Why, the very fact that so far our shores have remained' inviolate at the hands of the enemy is the best possible answer to those who ask why we should do this. Hon. gentlemen may recall that when the billion dollar bill was before parliament on March 18 of last year I reminded them of this:
For generations before this war began Britain has been guarding our sea lanes and our trade routes and providing protection for our very existence, all without any cost to us.
Now that Canada has arrived at man's estate, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) suggests; now that we are seeking to play the part of a great belligerent nation, it behooves us to pull our full weight in the great struggle now going on. I have been careful not to say anything, but I have sometimes wondered how it is that the Canadian army has not yet had an opportunity to pull its full weight in this war. I do not pretend to allot responsibility, but the fact remains that the Canadian army as such has not been in action as yet. I know how-restless some of the personnel of the Canadian army are because of that fact, and I happen to know further that it is not very pleasant for

I just throw out that suggestion in the hope that when the war estimates are up the Minister of National Defence will give the Canadian people at least some explanation why Canadian armed forces have not seen action.

It should not be necessary to repay for the billion dollars worth of goods in one year. But over a period of time Great Britain would repay in goods, and the Canadian people would have the money with which to buy the goods, because the government would repay the loan at that time. However, I shall deal with that aspect of the matter later on. I shall deal later on with the other suggestion the minister has made, because I wish to consider in sequence the points he raised the last time he spoke in the house respecting this measure.
He took exception to the suggestion that these goods might be made available in return for securities, namely, that the country might repatriate securities from Great Britain. On the point he said this:
Some might say, well; do not take I.O.U's; do not take sterling; do not have your cash drawer full of sterling; but exact securities; strip Great Britain of any securities she has. That sounds plausible. But what would we do with the securities? If we sold $500,000,000 worth of securities to the Canadian people, our sale of victory bonds would be decreased by $500,000,000. We would not have any more money in the treasury if we did that.
That does not appear to be a very logical argument. What is the purpose of selling $500 million worth of war bonds to the people? It is to curtail the spending of the people to that extent, and it is also to obtain $500 million from the Canadian people so that the government may spend it. On the other hand, it creates a debt of $500 million. But if we repatriate $500 million of securities from Great Britain, they could be sold to the Canadian people and we would have exactly the same result as if we sold $500 million of war bonds. In the first place we would curtail the spending power of the people by S500 million and. in the second

place, the government would have $500 million with which to buy war materials. And we would avoid going into debt to the extent of $500 million. The very argument presented by the minister is against his own policy. It would be of great advantage to sell $500 million of securities instead of selling $500 million of war bonds because we would be keeping out of debt to that extent.

I do not think so. I shall deal with some of the other points raised by the minister. I quite agree that we should make available to Great Britain or to any of the allied nations all the goods that we possibly can make available at this time. But I think that in every case where a country holds Canadian securities, those securities should first be repatriated. Then, when they have been repatriated we could continue to make goods available in the form of a gift, not merely for the duration of the war but for such time as it may be necessary to place that country upon its feet, which may be three or four years after the war.
The minister argues that it is necessary to give rather than sell in order to avoid interallied debts. But that works both ways. If it is disadvantageous to build up inter-allied debts, surely it is not to the advantage of any country to maintain debts already in existence. We should put first things first. Let us pay off the debts that exist, and then after they are paid off we can continue to make gifts so that no inter-allied debts may be piled up. The result of the minister's policy will be that at the end of the war, even though we may have given gifts to the extent of billions we may still be a debtor nation as far as certain countries are concerned. I think we should use this opportunity to pay off our debts. Then, when they are paid off, we can make goods available in the form of a gift.
The minister has stated that England holds something like $800 million of Canadian securities. From the information I have been given, I understand that these holdings are well over a billion dollars. Whether they are or not, I think we would be well advised to repatriate these securities at this time. By their being held in Great Britain instead of in Canada we are losing a considerable amount of revenue in the form of taxation which would be levied upon the holders of these securities. No doubt the minister will deal with this point when we are in committee. I should like to quote an editorial
[Mr. Queleh.l
which appeared in the Fundy Fisherman of March 3, 1943. It reads:
The only apparent reason that these investments are not brought back to Canada is that they enjoy a lesser taxation in England which is hardly fair, for there should be no holders of Canadian securities placed in a preferred position but the fault does not lie with the investor-it is ours. When substantial dividends are paid by these companies in Canada to their owners in England there are ways whereby these dividends may only be subjected to a single tax. Most of these companies are subsidiary companies, and once a tax is paid on their earnings there is no further tax that we know of, that is if the dividends remain in the treasury of the parent company.
Furthermore, even if paid out in dividends to shareholders, the method of taxing dividends in England is not nearly as severe as our method of full double taxation on dividends. Once a company pays a tax on their earnings the shareholder does not pay taxes again when the dividend is received from such company provided the taxpayer's bracket rate is lower than the company's rate. If higher, the shareholder just pays the difference.
If these securities were brought back to Canada our government could be sure of the full double taxation, the same as all Canadian investors pay. which would make taxation a little less on the rest of us.
As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar pointed out, the British people as a whole would not benefit by these securities not being repatriated. Those who would benefit are the holders of the securities. Generally speaking, these are some of the choicest of Canadian securities, such as Lever Brothers, Eno's, Hudson's Bay, Canadian Industries and Canadian Pacific Railway. European syndicates had large holdings in the diamond and gold mines of South Africa, but Great Britain purchased those holdings with sterling and charged them against the credits of South Africa held in the Bank of England. In that way South Africa has to a large extent eliminated absentee ownership. The Minister of Finance has stated that we have a credit in England of around $700 million. This could be used for the purchase of these securities, but we have no assurance that the government is going to purchase them. As a matter of fact, according to the argument presented by the Minister of Finance, this would be the last thing this government intends to do.
I am of opinion that Canada should follow the example of South Africa and repatriate these securities at the earliest possible opportunity. If this action is not taken, what guarantee have we that these securities will not be turned over to the United States under the lend-lease act? It is all very well to state that the lend-lease act is along the same lines as this resolution, but it is possible

The suggestion was made that British colonies should be turned over to the United States. We have no guarantee that in the next twenty years or so the same demand may not be made, that certain colonies should be turned over as payment for goods supplied during the war.

Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Air. Speaker, this is another very important measure. The resolution is divided into four paragraphs. The amount that is to be disposed of is $1,000,000,000, or in External Affairs language, one thousand million dollars. I do not see the importance of the distinction, but some people say that it is very important to use that nomenclature in discussing high finance.
Under the second paragraph of the resolution the governor in council may determine the terms and conditions upon which the war supplies purchased with the aforesaid sum are to be made available to any of the united nations, and the governor in council may require in certain cases payment or repayment in kind or property or reciprocal action or provision of supplies or other direct or indirect benefit as may be deemed appropriate. According to the fourth paragraph, the governor in council may be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, such sum or sums of money not exceeding in the whole the sum of one thousand million dollars.
I am opposed to each one of these proposals. It is not because I do not feel that this country should do the best possible to help our allies-not at all. It is just a matter of business and sense. Last year we voted the resolution to make a gift of one thousand million dollars to Great Britain. I stand by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), but I cannot understand why we have not a detailed account of the first gift which was made last year and the supplementaries which we voted early this session. This is the first reason why I am opposed to the first paragraph, namely, that we have no rendering of account of what was done last year. It is not because I am anti-British. I am giving the reasons. We used to have

I am strictly in order and I do not want any interruption from anyone but you, sir, because the time at my disposal is very short and I am not going to indulge in any blah-blah discussion. I have something more serious to say.
It was said this afternoon that lend-lease is not a loan of money, nor is it an act of charity. I concede that. I cannot understand, however, how it can be said of the gift that we made last year. The statement was made in the United. States about the lend-lease, but last year the policy was mot one of lend-lease; rather it was to make a free gift. The question that is now before the house is vital, not only for the present time and for the obligations we are now assuming but especially from the point of view of the post-war period.
Let me quote what was said recently in the proud city of Hamilton by a prominent Canadian journalist:
Mr. Grattan O'Leary stressed the importance of export trade to Canada, declaring that we must export or we die.
That is perfectly true, and I distinctly remember the stand I had to take with the party on the Ottawa agreements, complaining that those policies were injurious not only to this country and to the other dominions, but also to Great Britain itself. What struck me this afternoon was the magnitude of our effort not only in sending materials, not only in sending munitions, not only in sending supplies to Great Britain and the other allied nations, but also in making such enormous financial sacrifices for Great Britain and the other nations as well.
I am concerned about the statement that was made this afternoon by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), and I will tell him that a statement like that may be made to the house, but the debate must be adjourned in order, as was suggested by the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), to give every member an opportunity to read it carefully and to understand it thoroughly.

Mutual Aid Bill
I listened as well as I could to what the minister said although it was pretty dry. It was like a budget speech. You understand a budget speech only when you read it; you cannot understand it when it is delivered. This is the same, and it was very hard to follow the minister closely. Therefore I crave your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, if my references are not strictly accurate, and if there is a shade of difference between what was said and the note I took of it.
With regard to meat, war supplies, according to the Mutual Aid bill that will follow this, include farm products and raw materials, and therefore meat is included. If meat was not shipped to Russia before, it will be after this; therefore it is in order to speak of it. In the second place, the government proposes to enter into whatever reciprocal arrangements are practicable, under which our allies will furnish us with supplies or [DOT] services in return for what we provide. This, sir, is of the utmost importance because it corroborates what was said in the United States about lend-lease. It is the principle of lend-lease itself that we do not give away something as we did last year, but that we give something with the idea of getting something else in return, which is only fair when it can be done. It has also been said that the government desires to avoid piling up huge war debts by sending our supplies to our allies for payment after the war. Effective use of war supplies in the prosecution of the war may be deemed good and sufficient consideration for their transfer. Moreover, we intend, where any terms and conditions are provided for, to have them clearly specified at the time of transfer. This also is a consequence of the principle that the lend-lease act is not charity. We may expect something in return.
It is said that we shall deal directly with various countries. Last year we dealt with Russia through England, and now we will deal directly with the countries concerned. We have done a lot. The Minister of Finance has pointed out what we have done for Great Britain and the other allied nations and it was a summary of the part played by Canada in her policy as a good ally. Part of the statement made by the Minister of Finance had a very strong smell of Rasminsky, that fellow who was an official of the League of Nations and is now assistant to the chairman of the foreign exchange control board. It smells of the League of Nations, and it smells of Rasminsky. I do not believe much in the accomplishments of the League of Nations, which had the distinction of being
twice declared dead, once by Lord Baldwin and the second time by Mr. Chamberlain, without having been resuscitated in the meantime. This has the Rasminsky perfume. The minister said:	[DOT]
We have provided assistance to Britain not only to meet her own requirements but also to meet those of the rest of the sterling area. . . .
Not only do we help finance Great Britain and the British dominions; now we include the empire of India and the British colonial empire, not only the dominions but also the colonies, as well as "certain other middle eastern areas." We are financing the whole world. Imagine that; beggars financing the world! We make sacrifices to help the cause of the allies, but this kind of finance is most dangerous because the more you do in this way, the closer you bring us to annexation. I do not want annexation; I want to stay within the British empire, but I want this country to be as autonomous within the empire as it has been described by Mr. Bennett and by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Now we are to help the Dutch West Indies, and places like that. Then the minister said:
The dollar exchange resources of Britain and the rest of the sterling area are pooled. Parts of the sterling area which receive a surplus of dollar exchange from operations with Canada turn that surplus in to this pool and when they require dollars for expenditures in Canada they obtain them from this pool.
What kind of finance is that?
The foreign exchange control systems of the various parts of the sterling area are more or less unified for this purpose.
Not those of the British empire or of the British commonwealth of nations, but the exchange control systems of the sterling area. First it was the British commonwealth of nations, then the British empire, and now we have the sterling area that we are to finance.
Moreover, we have provided goods to Russia through Britain inasmuch as Britain made direct arrangements with Russia . . . and we have provided Britain with some of these supplies which she in turn has passed on to Russia in accordance with the terms qf her protocol.
