On those occasions details can be examined, scrutinized and debated.
There are, however, one or two observations I wish to make respecting the principle of the resolution before us. After what I have heard said in the house to-day I hope I shall not be regarded as old-fashioned if I rise in my place to say a word with respect, not only to what Canada is doing in the war, but what Great Britain herself has done. I believe it is not old-fashioned to make observations of that kind, and I hope it will never be so considered.
I believe a serious question was raised when the suggestion was made that Great Britain is not appreciative of what Canada has done in this conflict. I do not suppose there is a person in the whole of the British isles who not only is appreciative but understands the position which Canada has taken in respect of its war effort, and is appreciative to the full of all Canada has done and will do. I believe truly that a realization of what Great Britain and the British people have done in this war, to date, is something more than an expression of sentiment.
As I rise this evening to take part in this debate I cannot help recalling, as every hon. member must, those dark days of the spring of 1940, and then again in September and October of that year when the air force of Great Britain, assisted as it was by those from other places, was able finally to turn back the enemy. A great statesman, the number one statesman of the world, if you like, paid a tribute to those brave men of the clouds when he said, " Never in the history of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few." Those men were fighting, not just for the people of Britain, not just for the people of any particular part of the world, but for all of us. It was there where the fighting was. I think it is inappropriate to talk about balanc-
Mutual Aid Bill

ing accounts in a time of war such as this one, no matter whether it is with regard to this country or any other of our allies.
This is not the time to talk of making a bargain with those who are fighting as our partners. We are in this struggle together, and it seems to me that it is up to this country to do its utmost. The only limitation should be our capacity as a nation to provide to the utmost of our ability. That is the issue which faces us with respect to this Mutual Aid bill. May I point out again that it is not a matter of a gift by the Canadian people. I take issue with those who said last year that it wras a gift so far as Great Britain was concerned. These are not days of gifts; these are days when everyone puts forward his very last ounce of energy, whether physical, financial or otherwise. I want to announce, at least with respect to the principle of this measure, my support of the Progressive Conservative party. This is our stand regardless of what may be said with respect to the details of the measure. In so far as the principle involved in the broad resolution is concerned, I think it is our duty as an opposition to support the government to the fullest extent.
However, I wish to say to the minister and to the government that we should have a more comprehensive explanation of why this change has been made with respect to distribution. Last year the government was very loud and convincing in its arguments as to why these goods should be dispersed in the manner proposed, but within twelve months or so another scheme for the spending of this money is announced. At the appropriate time I should like the minister to give a more detailed and convincing answer to the question which was propounded and to tell us why the change envisaged by this resolution and the bill to be founded thereon was made.
When the minister makes his statement I should like him to give us some idea as to how these products and materials will be distributed. I realize that to a large extent this will depend upon the requirements of the various nations which are to be helped, but I think we ought to have some idea of what the government has in mind and where the bulk of this money is likely to go. I also wish to ask the minister-I asked him before when this matter was brought up in the house-if this Mutual Aid project is the result of collaboration between Great Britain, the United States, China, Russia and Canada. I think we ought to know whether Canada is simply acting on her own. In these days it is difficult to understand how any nation which is fighting a war in partnership with other nations can act alone.

This nation is bound up with many others which are fighting a common war and common battle for the preservation of our treasured way of life, and I should like to know wffiether conferences or conversations or discussions were held which led up to this Mutual Aid arrangement. I should like to know whether Great Britain has been consulted with respect to the change contemplated by this legislation. That is a point w'hich must be raised at the appropriate time and which must be answered by the minister.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks I rose only to place the stamp of approval of our party upon the principle of the measure which has been submitted, reserving the full right to criticize those details which in our opinion may be found faulty as the legislation progresses through its various stages. Our position is not one of opposition; it is one of support of the bill contemplated by this resolution. But in keeping with our traditional duty as His Majesty'sLoyal Opposition, we will insist upon every dollar of this money being spent efficiently and without waste and that the goods and services to be covered by the bill be distributed in the manner best calculated to contribute most to the defeat of the common foe.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the risk of having my attitude misrepresented in certain sections of this country and in this house, I cannot resist the desire to express at the outset of the discussion my point of view in connection with this most important measure. I would have waited for the presentation of the bill to state my own views on the matter, but the acceptance of a resolution of this kind means to a large extent the approval of the principle of the bill to be founded thereon, and therefore I feel that I should now express in a general way my personal opinion on the subject.
I am strongly opposed to the continuation of what may be called the colonial tribute of Canada. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said this afternoon that he was glad to see that Canada was now looking after her own affairs, without going through the offices of the British government, as was done last year. I do not know whether I am pessimistic, Mr. Speaker; I may be. At all events what I have seen happening in this house and in this country since the beginning of the war induces me to think that while we may be more independent in a legal sense since the passing of the Statute of Westminster, in practice wre have made, no progress at all, not one step forward in developing our autonomy and becoming a

Mutual Aid Bill
really independent country. We may glorify ourselves in the terms and words of the Statute of Westminster, but our practice remains the same. We seem to be happy to continue in the position of a country always ready to pay tribute and unable to exercise its autonomy.
Listening to the speeches that have been delivered in this house since the presentation of this resolution, one would be inclined to think that up to the present time Canada has not made any contribution to the war, that we have been derelict in our duty, that we have not taken our proper share of the burdens of this war. Nobody has said a word about what has been done by Canada. All those who have spoken have said that we should contribute more and more. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) suggests that we have not done enough, and that we should make a greater financial effort. One hon. member said during the discussion this afternoon that one billion dollars is not sufficient; that we should give more, as though in reality Canada had done nothing at all since the beginning of the war. They forget that we have hundreds of thousands of soldiers under arms at the present time and also forget that we have on the order paper, besides this one billion dollar resolution, another resolution calling for $3,890,000,000 to cover Canada's expense this year. Adding those two together to our ordinary expenditures we have a budget of $5,600,000,000 for a small country like Canada. No wonder that Mr. Churchill is amazed when he considers the contribution of Canada to the war! No wonder that Mr. Anthony Eden was surprised and could hardly grasp the magnitude of the war effort Canada is making! No wonder that the secretary of the treasury of the United States has said that the United States is far behind Canada so far as taxes are concerned! No wonder that newspaper's all over Canada have lately established the fact that we are more heavily taxed in Canada than any other country participating in the war!
The Minister of Finance when introducing the budget said that it was not a good way of measuring Canada's war effort to compare our taxation with that of other countries. What should be considered, said the Minister of Finance, is what is left to a country after the taxes have been paid. This is the rule, said the Minister of Finance, that should be applied in appreciating Canada's war effort. I am ready to follow that rule. I am ready to judge Canada's war effort from that point of view. I say that when everything is taken into consideration there is less left to Canada
than to any of the major countries participating in this war. We have not the same interests, we have not the same advantages in sight when the war is over that other countries have. Canada has no colonies; Canada has no territory over which she exercises sovereignty. Canada gained nothing from the last war, and Canada stands to gain nothing, materially speaking, from the present war. All the other countries taking part in this struggle have much more at stake than has Canada, and, due to the courses they have previously followed are much more responsible for the conflict in which we are now suffering. Canada has been acting like a colony. In the last twenty-five or fifty or one hundred years we have never been the cause of a war. But other countries, through their policies, through their trade and their attitude may have been responsible for the difficulties in which the civilized world finds itself to-day.
Reference has been made to the League of Nations. Who is responsible for the failure of the League of Nations. Who is responsible for the development of armaments in Germany? Not Canada. Canada is not responsible for the development of her strength or for permitting her to become one of the mightiest nations of the world.
We are in this war as a result of our free decision, I admit. But speaking frankly, man to man, where is the Canadian who would tell me that Canada would be at war to-day if England had not first gone to war? I participated in the declaration of war by Canada, and I have no regrets. I thought we should do something to help the allied nations. But I maintain that there are limits, there should be limits, to our participation.
I hear an hon. gentleman say, no. I may say to him that there are limits in some of the countries which will be leaders when the treaty of peace is signed. Canada will not be one of those leaders. We shall sign the treaty as we signed the one that concluded the last war, but we shall not be responsible for the terms which will be found in that treaty. Our signature will be found upon it only in approval of what will have been decided by the four great nations the names of which always come to the lips of those who are leading those four nations.
Canada plays a secondary role in this war, and will play a secondary role when the treaty of peace is drafted, and we are paying more in taxes and more in general expenditures toward this war than any other country. We have, in proportion to our population, more soldiers in arms, and we have more extensively controlled or brought into the war service our diversified industrial activities.
Mutual Aid Bill

When I say-and nobody can deny it- that we in Canada are paying more taxes than are being paid elsewhere, is that not the best evidence that there are limits elsewhere? If there were no such limits other countries would pay higher taxes than we, and it should be so because they have a greater interest in the conflict and in its consequences.
Mr. Speaker, the motion which is presented to us is really a repetition of what was approved last year. It is a gift just the same, although under a different name. But applying a new label to a bottle does not change the contents. We were helping other nations last year; we are going to help them this year in the same way.	[DOT]
It is true that, according to paragraph 2 of the resolution which is to be considered in committee, -we shall be empowered to claim certain advantages, certain compensations, certain payments for the advances we shall make. But one had only to listen to the observations of our brilliant Minister of Finance to understand very easily that he does not count at all on the compensations which can be obtained. He does not count on the supply of any goods which could be furnished us by other nations with whom we are associated. He repeated several times that this was our contribution to the common cause, our contribution to the successful continuation of the war against the axis powers.
It is a gift that wre are making. And to my mind it is no use appointing a new commission to determine what kind of guarantees or what sort of payments we will exact for the advances we shall make. The bill cannot be two things; it cannot be at the same time a gift and a sale. In reality it is a gift, and the future will disclose that we are only repeating what was done last year.
It is to be regretted that the house has not been given the advantage of a complete list of the expenditures covered by the advance of one thousand million dollars which we made to England last year. It might have been interesting. I do not know whether I understood aright the Minister of Finance when he made this statement. He is restricted by the censorship, said he, in issuing such a statement, and he now confirms my understanding.
Well, I cannot conceive that the government of Canada will be restricted, in supplying such information as that, by a body which it has created. The censorship board, composed of employees of the government, servants of the crown, are to limit the liberties, the powers and the authority of parliament

and prevent the Minister of Finance from giving details and information as to where our money has gone! I cannot subscribe to that. Surely we are not fighting for such a system. Surely the allied nations are not fighting to establish such a practice in the world. There should be a limit to the power given to these commissions and boards which are only creatures of the government and which should exist, not to hide information, but to help to publish public information,, as is done in other countries.
Am I mistaken in saying that to-day or yesterday the United States authorities published a long statement of the payments made and goods supplied to various countries under the lease-lend act? The information was given in detail in the United States. Here in Canada we cannot obtain it. Poor old statute of Westminster, where are you? Where has it gone? I can imagine no good reason at all to justify the statement made by the Minister of Finance as regards the limitation, by a board of censors, of his power to give details of this kind.
At least, if we are to pay another tribute, another colonial tribute, let us have the courage to repatriate the Canadian securities which are held in England. I cannot admit the soundness of the proposition that we should be generous to the point of giving our national and industrial products to another partner in the war and yet be shy about asking for the transfer of our securities. I cannot understand an attitude of that kind; it is beyond my poor imagination.
If we are to give money to other countries, let us repatriate, as the United States did, as a colony did, as India did, all our securities held in England. South Africa also repatriated all securities which were held there. There was a balance in the banks of England in favour of South Africa; pounds were there accumulated, and they were used to buy for the benefit of South Africa the securities which were held in England. Nobody accused them of being unpatriotic.
In India the transaction was carried through by a man, a Britisher, coming from England, and he was proud of what he had done for the country. Moreover, when the soldiers of India go outside the limits of their territory to fight for the united nations they are paid by the British treasury, not by the treasury of India. That is what is being done by a dependency.
But in Canada, a dominion, with our statute of Westminster, we are shy about bringing here our securities to help strengthen our credit and accumulate the funds needed for the continuation of our war effort.

Mutual Aid Bill
I cannot understand such a method of reasoning; nor can I understand, as is argued, that it would hurt us if we cease to be a debtor. I am not a financier, but I believe that it is only common sense that a man or a country is in a better position when a creditor rather than a debtor. I believe that if Canada had no debts at all she would be in a better position than she is now, with a burden of debts to many countries.
As regards protecting our trade, it is argued that the people of England will be more inclined to trade with us if they are creditors of Canada. Well, the people who will deal with Canada, the people who will buy our grain, the people who will buy our manufactured products in England will not always be the holders of Canadian securities. Those who will be interested in buying our grain and our manufactured products will not care much if a handful of people in England possess Canadian securities, or if certain banks or corporations are the holders of such securities.
That is not a businesslike argument. The English people will deal, as they have done in the past, where. it suits them best-first and last. They are a first-rate trading nation; and I admire them for that. They mind their own business; they know where their advantage lies, and they go and take it when they think it is time to reap that advantage. We ought to do the same thing; we ought to imitate them and try to reduce as much as we can the burden of our indebtedness and become a creditor country. The colony of India is at the present time a creditor country; South Africa is also at present a creditor country, and nobody accuses them of being unwise, and the inhabitants are not ashamed of their respective countries. My time is running short but there will be another opportunity for discussing this matter at greater length.
I wish to close by making reference to the sentimental observations made this afternoon by the ex-leader of the official opposition (Mr. Hanson). He was inclined to blame the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) because our soldiers are not yet in the field, because our soldiers are kept in England, not having yet taken as glorious a part as the soldiers of South Africa and others have taken in the north African campaign. Well, I am proud enough of my country to be also anxious and desirous to see as much glory as possible fall upon the heads and shoulders of our sons in any battle or fight such as the one in which Canada is now engaged. But as has been said, our soldiers in England are at present performing a useful task. They are there because the military authorities have
decided that they shall stay there, and they are rendering a veiy useful service not only to England but to the allies as well. I prefer the advice and the attitude of the military authorities, who are leading the British and the United States forces, to the sentiments expressed by my hon. friend.
I am not anxious to see a repetition of Dieppe, glorious as that was, so far as sacrifices are concerned. I am not anxious to see a spearhead made of the Canadian army at present in England. It may happen. I hope, from the bottom of my heart, from the bottom of my soul, that God will prevent such a thing from happening and that circumstances will be such that our sons will not be obliged, will not be forced to take the same position, to go into the same adventure as those who were at Dieppe. I hope we shall win the war, I hope our arms will be successful, without our sons who are at present in England being forced, for the sake of glory, for the vanity of glory, to be butchered as a number of our sons were butchered on the shores of Dieppe.
I repeat, I am not as anxious as the ex-leader of the opposition to see such a catastrophe take place. If it can be delayed, the longer it is the better it will be to me; and if it never came I would thank God for protecting our sons from such an adventure and for settling the problems of the world without exposing our sons as some of them were exposed at Dieppe.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words in connection with paragraph 4 of the resolution, and at the end of my remarks I will move an amendment. As I said in my speech on the budget, we are facing this year the heaviest budget we have ever had in this country, amounting to $5,500,000,000. Everyone has been wondering where the government is to get all this money. It is true that the government has not raised the rate of taxation on income, but anyone can hear numerous complaints about the large amounts deducted from weekly earnings. These complaints come especially from the heads of families, who cannot accept the minister's point of view, when he tried some time ago to explain to the people of Canada that it was not the duty of the state to provide the heads of families with the necessary means whereby to raise their children.
Mutual Aid Bill

They never thought so, but they do complain that the system of taxation is inequitable.
The first paragraph of the resolution before us provides that sums not exceeding one thousand million dollars be granted to His Majesty for the purpose of making war supplies available to any of the united nations, and paragraph 4 provides that the governor in council may be empowered to raise, by way of loan, this amount of money. The Minister of Finance has already tried to explain to the people of Canada that the effect of providing the united nations with war materials to the extent of one billion dollars is of great advantage to the country. It was said that it was better for us to give those goods rather than to sell them. I should like to be able to agree with that contention, but I always understood that when a merchant gives his goods to a customer instead of selling them it is not considered a very sound way of doing business. I also believe that after the war the representatives of this country at the peace conference would find themselves in a much better position if they held in their hands some credit notes from other nations taking part in the conference.
I wish to discuss another aspect of the question. Even if I could admit the minister's point of view, I could not set aside the fact that if the government borrows money under paragraph 4 of the resolution we shall have to pay interest on that money; taking the average rate of interest at three per cent, this government will have to pay about $30,000,000 a year in interest on this $1,000,000,000. Furthermore, according to the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act of 1931, to which this paragraph refers, we shall have to refund this money in the manner provided. Section 8 of chapter 27 of 21-22 George V deals with the *manner of raising loans, and section 9 reads as follows:
Upon authorizing the issue of securities under the last preceding section the governor in council may provide for a special sinking fund with respect to such issue, and may, at any time, provide for a general sinking fund for all such portions of the securities as have been or are hereafter issued without provision for a sinking fund: Provided that the amount to be invested in any such sinking fund shall not exceed one-half of one per centum per annum on the amount of the securities to which it relates.
This means that every year for the next 200 years the citizens of this country will have to pay about $35,000,000 on account of this loan. It also means that every citizen of this country living to-day, and everyone living in this country for the next 200 years, each week will see his pay envelope reduced to enable the

government to pay the interest on this loan. I believe the government should seek another way of raising this money if it is absolutely necessary for the success of the war in which we are now engaged. My contention is that for the duration of the war equality of sacrifice should be not only a phrase but a fact. No one should be permitted to increase his wealth through and by means of war. If during the war the government borrows five, six or ten billion dollars, it follows that somebody will hold those bonds; and according to the experience of the past the greater part of those bonds are bought and held by only a few people. A few million dollars worth are bought by the people at large, but that does not amount to very much in comparison with the whole. Not very long ago I heard the Minister of Finance complain in this house because some people had been selling their bonds instead of keeping them. Therefore I do not think I am wrong when I state that only a few people, firms, companies and societies will hold their government bonds after the war.
Further, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the government should apply the law that was adopted by this house in 1940. I refer to chapter 13 of 4 George VI, which was adopted in June, 1940, and which was known as bill No. 43. I quote from the preamble:
Whereas it is, therefore, expedient to confer upon the governor in council special emergency powers to permit of the mobilization of all of the effective resources of the nation, both human and material, for the purpose'of the defence and security of Canada. . . .
Section 2 reads as follows:
Subject to the provisions of section three hereof, the governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, requiring persons to place themselves, their services and their property at the disposal of his majesty in the right of Canada, as may be deemed necessary or expedient for securing the public safety, the defence of Canada, the maintenance of public order, or the efficient prosecution of the war, or for maintaining supplies or services essential to the life of the community.
In my opinion, when it is a question of raising men, this law seems to work very well, and I wonder why it should be altogether different when it is a question of raising money. This law places the property of every Canadian citizen at the disposal of the government. Therefore I should like the government to apply this law as it stands. Why did the government ask the House of Commons to adopt this law if it is not to be applied? Why does the government apply this law when it requires men but does not apply this law when it requires money? Therefore, in accord-

Mutual Aid Bill
ance with the provisions of this statute, I move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Gaspe:
That section 4 of the present resolution be amended as follows:
(a)	in substituting to the words: "Loan under the provision of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931";
the following words:
"Compulsory and proportionate raising from individuals, companies, firms, societies whose net assets are over $500,000;"
(b)	in striking out the last part of said section which reads as follows: "The principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would refer to paragraphs 440 and 441 of Beauchesne's " Parliamentary Rules and Forms," third edition, 1943, which read as follows:
440.	The fundamental terms of a money resolution submitted to the house with the governor general's recommendation upon which a committee of the -whole is set up cannot be amended. Amendments will only be in order if they fall within the terms of the resolution. The procedure in committee on those resolutions follows in principle the procedure of the committee of supply, and amendments are out of order if they are proposed with a view to substituting an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation.
441.	During the debate on a resolution to raise by way of loan under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, an amount not to exceed $750,000,000 for paying and redeeming certain loans and purchasing unmatured securities, a member moved in amendment that part of the loan be raised by the issue of currency by the government of Canada. The Chairman ruled the amendment out of order on the ground that it was proposed with a view to substituting an alternative scheme to that proposed with the governor general's recommendation. An appeal was taken to the house which confirmed the Chairman's ruling by a vote of 85 to 16.
442.	Amendments proposing, in a money resolution, to substitute a loan for a subsidy; to change the destination, purpose and conditions of a subsidy; attaching a condition to a subsidy; affecting the ends' and provisions of a subsidy, must be moved by a minister with the recommendation of the crown.
There may be other citations on the same page, but this seems to be pretty well within the principle of those citations. It is here proposed to substitute a compulsory loan or tax-if I understand it correctly, I believe it is a loan-on persons whose net assets are over S500,000. That is to be substituted for the payment of the billion dollars out of the consolidated revenue fund. I thought the words came in after "1931", but apparently the proposal is to take out the words, "loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931" and insert the 72537-157
words, "compulsory and proportionate raising from individuals, companies, firms, societies whose net assets are over $500,000." So that the section would read:
That the governor in council may be empowered to raise by way of compulsory and proportionate raising from individuals, companies, firms, societies whose net assets are over $500,000, such sum or sums of money not exceeding in the whole the sum of one thousand million dollars as may be required for the purpose of defraying the expenditures herein mentioned and for purchasing or otherwise acquiring or procuring war supplies in Canada.
In other words, a most important taxation provision is grafted on to this resolution.

speechtext:
It appears to be taxation.
It refers to "compulsory and proportionate raising from individuals, companies, firms, societies whose net assets are over $500,000." I think it would be a tax. It is a tax on a certain class, until the billion dollars would be obtained. It is entirely unworkable, but I am not pressing that point. My point is that the proposal has been made to substitute an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation.

speechtext: I wonder if the minister is right in his interpretation of the amendment. The suggested words are, "compulsory and proportionate raising from individuals" and so on. Does the hon. member offering the amendment not leave wide open the question as to whether it is a tax or a compulsory loan? I do not know just what this means, whether it is intended to be a capital levy or a compulsory loan. If it is ruled out on the ground that it is a tax, it is subject to the interpretation of a compulsory loan. I submit that the question whether it is a loan or a tax can be clarified, if the committee approves it, in the discussion on the bill. It seems to me there is some doubt as to whether the amendment, in its present terms, is out of order. Does the striking out of the words, "the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund," not imply that this is an interest-free loan rather than a tax?

speechtext:
I shall read paragraph 4
of the resolution, as amended:
That the governor in council may be empowered to raise by way of compulsory and proportionate raising from individuals, companies, firms, societies whose net assets are over $500,000 such sum or sums of money not exceeding in the whole the sum of one thousand million dollars as may be required for the purpose of defraying the expenditures herein mentioned and for purchasing or otherwise acquiring or procuring war supplies in Canada.

Mutual Aid Bill

That is the paragraph as it would read if the amendment were accepted. It is suggested with respect to this resolution that, having received the approval of His Excellency the Governor General, it is impossible to change it. His Excellency has approved a Mutual Aid bill for one thousand million dollars. But if the amendment were accepted, we would have a compulsory loan. And even if it were not called a loan, it would be the means of receiving money from a certain class of individuals better able to pay than any other class, because they have the money with which to pay. Therefore it is only sensible to suggest that the money should be levied from those who have the means to pay for such aid.
In conclusion, I wish to say that it is not important whether the money is to be raised by way of loan or by way of levy; that is, as far as authorization by his excellency is concerned. The duty of his excellency is to check the expenditure of the money, and he has graciously given his consent to the providing of means to raise this billion dollars. I am sure that his excellency has paid no attention at all to whether it is to be by loan or by levy; he has simply authorized it. Under the circumstances I am sure it would be most unfair to his excellency to contend that because loan is mentioned in the resolution we should not consider it as meaning levy as well, provided it is desirable to the committee to accept the amendment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I have just a word to say on the interpretation of the amendment, and I shall leave to the minister the task of taking exception to its being in order. I think it is quite clear from a careful reading of this proposal that the hon. gentleman is endeavouring to substitute a capital levy upon certain classes in Canada for a loan; he negatives the idea of a loan by paragraph (b). Mutual Aid Bill

Perhaps I should answer that because I have had rather intimate relations with the planning of the munitions programmes of the allied nations. The programmes of all the allied nations are closely integrated, and they are based on the principle that every nation shall do everything that it is capable of doing in the common cause. To integrate the efforts there, are a number of boards. I am a member of the combined production and resources board. That is a board made up of three men, the other two being Mr. Oliver Lyttelton, representing the United1 Kingdom, and Mr. Donald Nelson representing the United States. We each have a deputy, and the three deputies are in continuous session in Washington studying the planning of the war production of the united nations. There is a counterpart of the board in London, each having a deputy in London, and the board is sitting there viewing the situation from London. Advice on strategic needs is obtained from another joint board, the combined chiefs of staff board, and the combined chiefs of staff board have a committee sitting continuously in Washington and another committee sitting continuously in London studying the strategy of war and reporting on the need of weapons in the various war efforts. There is a combined materials board sitting in Washington with a counterpart in London, dividing up the materials of the world as they are required by the nations in their production programme. There is another board, the shipping board. All the shipping of the united nations is pooled in one pool and is assigned by the combined shipping board to the various routes. After all, production in any country is not available in another country unless there are ships to move that production.
The question is, what can Canada do? As I say, the underlying principle is that every nation shall do all it can. Is a nation entitled to help under the Mutual Aid bill or under the lease-lend bill of the United States? The position of the nation is looked at. Is the nation able to pay for its goods? If so,, it will pay for its goods up to its capacity to pay. That is the first qualification of any country. No country gets lease-lend or will get Mutual Aid if its circumstances are such that it is able to pay for the goods it
requires, or until it has paid* to the limit of its ability to pay. Is the other nation reciprocating? For example,, there may be troops stationed in that country. If it is able to do so, that country provides food for the troops, no matter to whom those troops may belong, and it may also provide clothing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
As Australia and Britain do
for the United States troops. That is the first and basic consideration. If the position of a nation is examined in that light and if it qualifies under that stipulation, it is a proper recipient of lease-lend from the United States or Mutual Aid from Canada or help from Britain.
How will the Mutual Aid of Canada be distributed? Requests will come in from various countries for the help they wish to obtain. Each request will be examined by the various coordinating boards. The chiefs of staff committee of Canada will consult with the joint chiefs of staff committee in Washington or London to determine whether the strategic needs of the war warrant- the export of goods to that particular area in the quantities suggested for Canada. Then the shipping board will report on whether shipping can be made available to transport goods from Canada to the area concerned. The combined production and resources board will report on whether it is really best for Canada to contribute that production. They may say, no, that it can be taken care of more easily from Britain with less shipping, that British production is quite capable of taking care of that requirement; or they may decide that the United States can better take care of it. But if they decide that Canada is the proper country to supply that particular need, that is another factor. Then the ability to pay is tested. What is the other country capable of doing? Is it doing all it can? Is it entitled to receive the goods entirely as Mutual Aid, or can it pay fifty per cent in Canadian funds, or can it pay some other proportion? All these things are tested through existing machinery, which is well oiled. and functioning smoothly. If a request meets all the tests, that country will be listed as a proper recipient of Mutual Aid.
I believe another question asked was why a billion dollars has been fixed as the proper-amount for Mutual Aid. This amount was fixed by the ability of Canada to produce,, less the amount involved in Canada's own commitments. We have armies overseas

the shipping of the allied nations. These matters have been coordinated to the point where we go to a central body and arrange transportation. I have gathered from him that there is coordination in respect of production and allocation through the joint board to which he has referred, on which Canada has adequate representation. I realize the representations in last year's legislation with respect to making direction contributions in kind to those of the allied nations other than Great Britain. I feel disposed to say that if there is any kudos coming to Canada because of giving direct to those nations in distress which we are seeking to help, and who are fighting part of a common cause, then so far as I am concerned Canada should have it. I think that is hardly true. Great Britain has taken the dominions under her wing. She clears all the bills. For example, Australia sends airmen to Canada. The bill for transportation of those airmen is paid by Great Britain. In the initial stages each country contributed so much per man. Great Britain is the clearing house for all countries in the sterling area. They may say, "All right, we will take up the slack." It may be that one country may have a surplus of sterling in Great Britain. In theory every country does what it can. If it has a sterling balance it might be perfectly proper, in an ordinary transaction, for it to pay for munitions, even if those munitions went from Canada to Great Britain. That is possible. I do not think it happens, but I would hesitate to say that it could not happen, under that arrangement. But to-day Great Britain buys from these countries, pays their bills, and more or less is the banker for the sterling countries. I think the hon. member has opened up a field which cannot be answered exactly from any information we have in this country.
I believe,, however, that Great Britain's course in her relationships with the dominions, both on balance and individually, will be entirely creditable. It will be found that Britain gives more than she gets in this war effort. I can say to the best of my knowledge and belief that Great Britain has spared absolutely nothing to win the war, and to protect British territory in every part of the world.

under the top level each board has representatives from every country. Every country is represented either in London or in Washington, and as such they sit on the subcommittees of the main boards. The boards are kept small so that they can act quickly, and I think there is everything to be said for that. You can walk into a board with an urgent situation and get an almost immediate decision. Every nation interested in a particular subject is represented.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I should like the Minister of Finance to clarify a word which he used in his speech this afternoon. The first clause of the resolution provides one billion dollars for

Mutual Aid Bill
the purpose of making war supplies available to any of the united nations. This afternoon the minister said, "united nations or associated nations" and I should like to know what nations are associated nations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I was not very careful in using that phrase, but the reason why it was used was the definition of "united nations" which appears in the bill. This definition reads:
"United nations" means the signatories to the declaration by united nations, done at Washington on the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and forty-two, and includes any other nation or authority which may be designated by the governor in council as being associated with Canada in the prosecution of the present war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: It occurred to me as being a strange use of the word by the minister in his speech. In connection with the war we are associated with certain nations in a way which in my opinion is not particularly to our credit and does not give any great hope for the future. Would Spain be considered an associated nation? I think that should be made very clear so that the people of Canada may be assured that this money will not be used for nations with which we may be associated unfortunately, which are not part of the united nations and which are not working for a united nations victory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Spain is not associated with Canada in the prosecution of the present war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: But she is getting supplies from the united nations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Not from Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Not very much, but a
little is going in.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver East has asked whether the terms "united nations" and "associated nations" are synonymous. I thought the minister might have taken a leaf out of his leader's book. The other day the Prime Minister was asked the difference between British empire and British commonwealth of nations, and he replied that they were interchangeable terms. Perhaps that answer could be given in this case. However, I did not rise for that purpose. I am rather alarmed-it is not the first time I have been alarmed over what the hon. member for Vancouver East has said-over the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I think he has said either too much or too little with regard to some of the nations with which we are associated in the common cause at this time. I think he ought to clarify the term which he used. I may be
innocent with respect to the matters involved in this struggle, but it does seem to me that this is the first time I have heard this particular matter raised.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I do not think I said either too much or too little. What I had in mind is what is in the minds of many people in Canada, the people with whom I come in contact. First, we are not dealing particularly with nations; we are dealing with individuals whose connections with the axis powers are not at all as they should be. There is a great deal of material going from this continent to Spain, and it is quite likely that it is finding its way to the axis powers. According to the return I received from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the quantity going from Canada is not much, but it may increase at any time as our trading relations increase. We have no control in this house because we can hardly get any information as to what trading we are doing with other countries. I wanted to be clear as to the meaning of the term "associated nations".

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Vancouver East intended to clear my mind with respect to this, but he has not. Has the hon. member any other nation except Spain in mind? He did not mention any other, but in his general discussion he rather left the impression that there were others.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Possibly I was thinking more of individuals than of nations.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
This year, according to
clause 2, we may require in certain instances payment or repayment in kind or property or reciprocal action. What would be the determining factor as to whether these goods would be made available in the form of a gift or for payment or repayment in kind?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: It depends entirely upon the ability of the recipient nation to pay. If it can deliver goods which Canada requires, those goods would be exacted. If it can pay in Canadian dollars, those would be exacted. If it cannot pay at all the goods would be made available as a gift; if it could pay something, the remainder over that would be made available as a gift. If it could pay in goods or in Canadian money, that would not eat into the billion dollars. That would be a commercial transaction. The Mutual Aid machinery will handle the transactions even though there is payment by the recipient country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: And there will be no discrimination between nations?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
No.
Mutual Aid Bill

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Will the minister
tell us whether the possibility of receiving payment or repayment in kind as indicated in clause 2 was an important factor in changing from the procedure followed last year whereby we donated the goods through Britain, while now we are donating them direct?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Under last year's arrangement we traded with many nations. Any nation that could pay us and needed the munitions was able to buy munitions here. That situation is unchanged. They can still buy here if they are able to pay for the munitions. But if the strategic needs of the situation require that we give munitions beyond the capacity of a nation to pay for them, we can give those munitions under this new bill. If they are able to pay for them, they will still pay for them under this bill as under the previous bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
My point is that
last year we gave one billion dollars to Great Britain, which in turn passed on the goods to other nations, from which we received or could receive nothing in return for any part of the billion dollars that we indirectly gave them. Under the terms of this year's measure we give the goods direct to the united nations and may receive from them in return some part of the billion dollars by way of repayment. Was that an important factor in introducing this change?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: No. We sold goods to many countries. We sold munitions to Russia, for instance, last year, for United States or Canadian dollars.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: That did not come under the gift?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
No. If it came under the
gift it had to be done through Britain. So far as purchases for cash by any nation are concerned, the situation is unchanged. We could always sell for cash and we can in the future.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I do not think my point is clear yet to the minister. Last year we gave a gift of one billion dollars for which we could hope to receive nothing in return. This year we are giving one billion dollars, and according to clause 2 we have hopes of receiving payment or repayment in kind for a portion of that billion dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
right to some extent. There may be goods which will have post-war usefulness which may be returned to us. I do not know

how far that will go. I imagine that might be the case with ships, for example. It would not be the case with shells. There might be some return in kind possible under this legislation which was not possible under that of last year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: The hon. member for York-Sunbury asked why the change of procedure this year from that of last year, why we are giving direct to the united nations under this legislation instead of through Great Britain. Is it the possibility of making a better business deal, whereby we may get by this means part of our billion dollars back? Was that a factor in making the change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will look at the speech I made this afternoon, he will see that I mentioned that as being a factor but I did not emphasize it as an important one.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Before this clause carries I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to the accounting in connection with the so-called billion dollar gift to Britain. It can scarcely be called that, but the minister will know from the description I have given what I have in mind. I take it from the statement he made this afternoon that there will be some accounting made to parliament with respect to the billion dollars allocated to Britain, showing how the money was actually spent. The minister made some reference, and some reference was also made by the member for Richelieu-Vercheres, to censorship. That brings me to this point. I have here a report to the 78th congress of the United States on lend-lease operations, the document from which the minister read, I think, this afternoon. It .covers the period from the passing of that legislation on March 11, 1941, to December 31, 1942, and contains a clear, not too long, and very informative description of the whole lend-lease arrangements of the United States with other countries. I was amazed to read the detail with which these operations are set out in this report, because for so long we have been told in this house that certain information cannot be given on account of the fact that there is some arrangement with respect to that matter between the united nations. I have not the time tonight to read to the committee some of the details on these lend-lease operations, but I strongly urge the government from now on not to use the time-worn argument that the nations with which we are fighting are in agreement with respect to making public certain information. This afternoon we had the odd situation of the minister suggesting that

Mutual Aid Bill
censorship in this country might prevent the giving of certain information to the people's representatives. Yet here is a report to congress of the lend-lease operations, setting them out in much more comprehensive fashion than is usually the case with respect to information given to us on ordinary expenditures. I am not suggesting that the minister will hide behind censorship. I think he is quite honest when he says there are perhaps reasons why some information cannot be given in full, but certainly we in this house are entitled to at least as much information as the United States congress receives with respect to operations under a similar measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Does that follow?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Why does the hon. gentleman assume that the practice of the United States of America is the right one in this case? The hon. gentleman is assuming that the practice of the United States of America is correct and that our practice is wrong. I do not know whether it is or not, but I do deny that we should slavishly follow the precedent set by congress or by the President of the United States or by others of yie allied nations. It is a provision of their legislation, passed when they were a neutral, that there must be a full report. That may give all kinds of information to the enemy which should not be given. I do not know whether it does or not; but what I am saying is that we should not, simply because they do that, do the same thing ourselves. I said this afternoon that I had not been able to agree to furnishing exhaustive information of the kind which was asked for-the number of tanks, the number of guns, and so on. I said that if I could I would present it. I was criticized by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres for admitting that the power of the minister or the government was subject to that of a board. I did not really think that was what I was doing. I thought I was respecting the censorship rules and regulations which have been established, and which ought to be respected unless they are deliberately overruled, I do not think we should be setting up an authority which lays down regulations, and then turn round and break them ourselves, unless there is a very good reason; and as at present advised, I would respect that attitude. Of course we have the power. We set up the censorship. We could pass an order in council overruling it for this purpose, but I do not know why we should.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
But the minister has
missed the point entirely. I think he has made a very good point from his own point of view. My argument has been this. We have been told through these war years that there is a reason why, for instance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce cannot bring down, under an order passed by the house, information in connection with exports from and imports to this country; that there is some agreement between the nations with respect to this. Well, if there is an agreement between the nations, are the United States part and parcel of the whole inter-allied structure? I do not know any reason why the information should be given by one government and withheld by the other. I am not asking that the government "slavishly"-to borrow the minister's term-follow some other government, but that this government give its people the same information which the government with which it has or is supposed to have this agreement is giving to its own people.
I do not want to hold the committee up longer, because it is very close to eleven o'clock. But I ask the minister, in the light of what the report to congress contained, and having in mind what he said this afternoon with respect to censorship, to let us have a full disclosure of what happened to the money which was voted before, so that we shall have some idea of the manner in which it was expended.
More than that, will the bill which will be founded upon this resolution provide for any report such as this to parliament with respect to the operations of the Mutual Aid project? This is a bulk sum. It provides a blank cheque. While you may not be so careful when you give a blank cheque, the facts are important when the question of accounting arises; and it is essential and necessary in the public interest.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
As one of the chief offenders against censorship, perhaps I may speak on this. The British take a different view of censorship from the Americans. The British have been longer in the war. They send out requests to Canada to preserve secrecy in certain matters. Unfortunately I can hardly talk about my own department without violating some of the rules, and I invariably get a call from the high commissioner pointing out that I have violated British rules of censorship. I do not like to do it, but I can hardly talk about our situation without doing so. After all, we have followed the British rules. The United States came in the war later. They took up lend-lease as a neutral
Mutual Aid Bill

country and passed a law which requires congress to be furnished with certain information. They have continued to do so, and possibly that information is of aid to the enemy. But their published statements represent only a part of allied production. If Britain, Canada and Russia also placed their information on the table, Germany would have a full and complete picture of allied production, and that might be a much more serious matter than a picture of United States production alone. I believe some high official of the United States government made the statement that the production picture is good and could give no comfort to the enemy. I think the allied picture is good and can give no comfort to the enemy. Nevertheless we have followed the British practice of withholding certain information which they think it wise to withhold.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Have we followed the British practice? My understanding is that in many of their secret sessions questions are asked as to what has been sent to China and Russia and other countries, and explicit statements are given of what is being done. We have not the United States plan, nor do we meet in secret session to find out where these expenditures are going. I personally much prefer the procedure of our parliaments to the procedure in the congress of the United States. It is much easier for us to seek information here than, apparently, it is possible for them, in view of the manner in which they have to refer matters to committees and get a motion through in order to have an inquiry made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Is it worse there than it is here?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I think it is as regards seeking day-to-day information. I believe that it takes much longer there, and that apparently we have an easier system of getting information by asking for returns and putting questions on the floor of the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: They can call officials to their committees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Nevertheless I think the minister is not quite correct in saying that we are following British procedure, because there have been frequent sessions in Britain at which information which they did not wish to be divulged, could not divulge, and the divulging of which would violate the censorship regulations of the country, is given to parliament in secret session. We are in this position to-night: all of us anxious, ready and willing to put this resolution through and make this appropriation and this gift-I think

we may use that term although it is criticized -but we do not know what was done with the money last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: You know the broad categories. You know the total.	.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: We know the broad categories and the total, but we do not know where it went. Of course we have been giving it to Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Yes; it all went to Britain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: What do we propose to do this year with this sum of money? Some of us have a great hope that this year China will get a great deal more than she has been getting during the last few years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: It is eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: The first part of the resolution provides for making supplies available to all the united nations. May I ask the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Munitions and Supply if under the War Measures Act or other act provision was not made for a credit to Russia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Russia has a credit for the purchase of wheat. That is the only order in council I know of.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: What is the amount of the credit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Ten million dollars. I do not know to what extent it has been used. I believe that six or seven million dollars has been used.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I may be mistaken, but I have a vague recollection that not very long ago the credit was increased quite substantially.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Oh, no. Just ten million dollars; that is all. There has been no reason for increasing it. It relates entirely to the purchase of wheat and flour, and the amount has not yet been used up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I repeat that I may be mistaken, but I thought the first order in council provided for a credit of around ten million dollars, and that a subsequent order in council, passed not very long ago, increased the credit to twenty-five million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: No; that is not correct. However, I will confirm that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I will look up my file and the order in council.

Radio Broadcasting

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: If I am wrong I will admit it to-morrow, but I never beard of a twenty-five million dollar credit.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Ten million dollars worth of grain is something.
